note: Chosen by the gap rather than by the list. The 2026-08-10 measurement showed the top-25 essentially complete on tree count (only Chicago short, by four) and 94 photographs short of the bar, with the whole shortfall concentrated in six cities: Boston 10 of 10 missing, Budapest 12 of 12, Copenhagen 13 of 13, Chicago 6 of 6, Washington DC 13 of 14, New York 15 of 20. Commons has nothing for these, proven by two viewing passes that judged 35 candidates and approved none. So these twelve go to the people who hold the actual trees. Same frame as batch 002: a compliment, what the site is for, then the ask for photographs, corrections and the tree we missed. No word about coverage or links.

mails.subject: Six of the ten Boston trees we publish are yours, and none has a photograph
mails.body:
Hello,

The Arboretum is the reason Boston has a tree list worth writing at all. Very few collections anywhere can put an accession card next to a tree, and the fact that the original American dawn redwood, grown from the 1948 seed, is still standing where it was planted is the sort of thing most cities can only claim.

My name is Hidde. I map the most remarkable old trees of cities at ancienttrees.app, each with its story, its exact spot and a walking route linking them. The point is not a catalogue: it is to give someone a concrete reason to go outside and stand in front of something that has been alive for a very long time.

We publish ten trees for Boston and six are yours, among them the Peters Hill white oak, the Franklin tree in the Explorers Garden, the original dawn redwood and the Wilson paperbark maple.

Two things would help enormously, and the first is what we need most. Do you have photographs of these trees we could use, credited however you ask? Not one of our ten Boston trees has an image, which is our largest gap and not one we can close from a desk. Second: have we got anything wrong, on the age, the accession or the spot, and is there a tree of yours that should be on this list and is not? Your accession records would settle in a line what we have had to infer.

The page is here: https://ancienttrees.app/boston

If you would rather not hear from me again, just say so and I will not write again.

Best wishes,
Hidde

mails.subject: The Shaw Memorial elms and the Public Garden dawn redwood, and a request
mails.body:
Hello,

The elms flanking the Shaw Memorial are among the very few American elms of that generation still standing in a city centre, and the fact that they are is not an accident: it is the tree care your organisation funds.

My name is Hidde. I map the most remarkable old trees of cities at ancienttrees.app, each with its story, its exact spot and a walking route linking them. The aim is to give someone a concrete reason to go outside and stand in front of something old, rather than read about it.

We publish ten trees for Boston, and the Common and Public Garden hold two of them: the Shaw Memorial elms and the dawn redwood.

Two questions, and the first is the one that would help most. Do you have photographs of these trees we could use, with the credit you prefer? Not one of our ten Boston trees carries an image, which is our biggest gap. And second: is there a tree on the Common or in the Public Garden that belongs on this list and is not there, or something we have written wrongly? Four centuries-old elms stand on the Common and we have struggled to tell them apart from a distance, which is exactly the kind of thing you would know in a sentence.

The page is here: https://ancienttrees.app/boston

If you would rather not hear from me again, just say so.

Best wishes,
Hidde

mails.subject: Eight of our twenty New York trees are in the Park, and we are short of photographs

My name is Hidde. I map the most remarkable old trees of cities at ancienttrees.app, each with its story, its exact spot and a walking route linking them. mails.subject: Chicago is the hardest city we have mapped, and we would value your help
mails.body:
Hello,

Chicago has been the hardest city on our list, and that is not a complaint about Chicago. It is a young city on old prairie, its remarkable trees are bur oaks that predate the street grid, and they are genuinely hard to find documented as individuals. The Illinois Big Tree Register is the one source that treats them as named specimens.

My name is Hidde. I map the most remarkable old trees of cities at ancienttrees.app, each with its story, its exact spot and a walking route linking them. The aim is to give someone a concrete reason to go outside and stand in front of something that was alive before the city was.

We publish six trees for Chicago: the Midway bur oak, the Wooded Island grove, the Union Ridge Cemetery savanna, the champion boxelder, the champion red pine and a witness oak in Oak Park. Six is fewer than any other major city on our site.

So two questions, and the second matters more here than anywhere. Do you have photographs of these trees we could use, credited however you ask? None of the six has an image. And which Chicago-area trees are we missing? You run the Chicago Region Trees Initiative and keep the Big Tree Register; if anyone knows which individual trees deserve a place, it is you, and we would rather be corrected than publish a short list.

The page is here: https://ancienttrees.app/chicago

If you would rather not hear from me again, just say so.

Best wishes,
Hidde
ancienttrees.app

mails.body:

My name is Hidde. I map the most remarkable old trees of cities at ancienttrees.app, each with its story, its exact spot and a walking route linking them. The aim is to give someone a concrete reason to go outside and stand in front of something that has been alive for centuries.
